title: Multi-dimensional data, sorted on one integer
description: Lindel — linearization and delinearization — maps coordinates to unsigned integer keys using Hilbert or Morton (Z-order) curves. Sort by the key when writing Parquet or loading tables to organize rows for queries that filter multiple dimensions.

sections.title: Organize rows across multiple dimensions
sections.description: Parquet readers use per-row-group min/max statistics to skip data that cannot match a predicate. Ordering by a space-filling-curve key can group nearby coordinates and make these statistics more selective across several columns. Results depend on the coordinate transform, data distribution, row-group size, and query filters. Neither tight bounds on every column nor smaller files are guaranteed.

sections.title: Hilbert and Morton
sections.description: Both curves map several integer coordinates to one sortable position. Compare their encoding cost and the resulting file layout on your data.

bulletPoints.label: Hilbert
bulletPoints.description: Follows a curve with no long jumps between consecutive positions on its integer grid. A useful starting point for locality-oriented sorting; nearby input points are not guaranteed to become adjacent rows.

bulletPoints.label: Morton / Z-order
bulletPoints.description: Interleaves the coordinate bits. The mapping is simpler than Hilbert but has jumps at quadrant boundaries.

bulletPoints.label: Supported inputs and output width
bulletPoints.description: Accepts integers, FLOAT, DOUBLE, BOOLEAN, DATE, TIME, TIMESTAMP, DECIMAL (up to 18 digits) and ENUM, as a fixed-size array or as separate arguments: 8-bit coordinates in 1–16 dimensions, 16-bit in 1–8, 32-bit in 1–4 and 64-bit in 1–2. The output is the smallest unsigned type that holds all coordinate bits, up to UHUGEINT.

sections.title: Prepare and decode coordinates deliberately
sections.description: Keys sort like the coordinates, including negative numbers, floats and dates. Choose the grid and units that match your queries.

bulletPoints.label: Quantize bounded values onto a grid
bulletPoints.description: hilbert_encode_latlon and hilbert_encode_bounded scale latitude/longitude or any bounded DOUBLE values onto 2^bits cells per dimension, giving dense keys from 0 to 2^(dimensions × bits) − 1. Wide types such as DOUBLE can be encoded directly, but spread their keys over 128 bits.

bulletPoints.label: Choose consistent units and ranges
bulletPoints.description: Set the scale of each dimension to reflect the precision and relative importance your queries need. Keep those choices consistent across files and batches.

bulletPoints.label: Decode with the original shape and key type
bulletPoints.description: Name the encoded type, such as hilbert_decode(key, 'DOUBLE[2]') or 'DATE[2]'. The original form takes the dimension count, return_float and return_unsigned; signedness must match the encoded values. Preserve the encoded key’s SQL type because its width determines the coordinate width.

bulletPoints.label: A write-time ordering
bulletPoints.description: Apply ORDER BY inside COPY to persist the layout. Queries still filter the original columns, and new batches need their own sorting. For key-only stores, hilbert_ranges turns a box into the key ranges to scan; inside DuckDB, a coordinate filter on curve-sorted data is faster.
